questions.question: A Surrey school has 500 students. A teacher asks 50 of them how they travel to school each morning. In this survey, what is the population?
options: All 500 students at the school
The 50 students who were asked
Every student in BC, since surveys need everyone
The students who ride the bus to school
questions.explain: The population is the whole group you want to know about, so here it is all 500 students; the 50 who answered are the sample. A common trap is calling the 50 answers the population.

questions.question: A Kelowna bakery makes 600 muffins one morning. The baker weighs 20 of those muffins to check they are the right size. What is the sample?
options: All 600 muffins made that morning
The 20 muffins that were weighed
Every muffin the bakery has ever baked
The average weight of one muffin
questions.explain: The sample is the small part actually measured, which is the 20 weighed muffins, while the 600 muffins are the population. Do not swap the two groups.

questions.question: A company makes 8000 bike helmets. Testing one helmet means crushing it until it cracks, so that helmet is ruined. Why does the company test only 40 helmets?
options: Because 40 helmets are the same as all 8000
Because every helmet should be crushed and checked
Because testing every helmet would destroy them all
Because helmets that are not tested cannot break
questions.explain: When a test destroys what it measures, a sample is the only sensible choice; crushing all 8000 would leave the company nothing to sell.

questions.question: A radio station wants to know what fraction of the 5 million people in BC liked a new song. It phones 800 listeners instead of everyone. Why?
options: Because 800 listeners are the same as 5 million
Because a song can only be judged by 800 people
Because everyone in BC should be phoned one by one
Because phoning 5 million people costs far too much
questions.explain: Sampling is sensible when a census would cost too much money or take too much time; phoning 5 million people is not realistic, so 800 listeners give an estimate.

questions.question: In a Victoria neighbourhood of 1200 homes, 60 homes are asked about recycling and 45 of them say yes. Which conclusion is correct?
options: About 75% of the 1200 homes likely recycle
Exactly 45 of the 1200 homes do recycle
Exactly 75% of the 1200 homes recycle, for sure
All 1200 homes must be asked before any guess
questions.explain: 45 out of 60 is 75%, so about 75% of the 1200 homes likely recycle. A sample gives an estimate for the population, never an exact fact about it.

questions.question: A cereal company checks that boxes hold 500 g by pouring out and weighing the contents, which ruins the box. It fills 20 000 boxes a day. What should it do?
options: Weigh every box, since all boxes must be checked
Weigh 100 boxes and estimate the rest from them
Weigh 100 boxes and call that the exact daily total
Weigh no boxes, because 20 000 is too many
questions.explain: When the check destroys the product, test a sample and use it to estimate the whole batch; weighing every box would empty all 20 000 the company wants to sell.

questions.question: A biologist studies the fish in a lake. She nets 20 fish, measures each one, then releases them. Which statement names the groups correctly?
options: The 20 netted fish are the population studied
Every fish must be netted to name a population
All the fish in the lake are the population
The lake itself is the sample being measured
questions.explain: The population is the whole group of interest, all the fish in the lake, and the 20 measured fish are the sample. Netting every fish in a lake is not possible.

questions.question: At a Coquitlam school with 900 students, the chess club surveys its own 30 members and 24 want a longer lunch. The club posts “Four out of five students at our school want a longer lunch.” What is the biggest problem?
options: The fraction 24 out of 30 is not four out of five
They must survey all 900 students, which is always possible
Nothing is wrong, since 30 members stand for the school
Chess club members do not represent all 900 students
questions.explain: 24 out of 30 really is four out of five, so the arithmetic is fine, but the sample came only from the chess club, so it is biased and cannot speak for all 900 students.

questions.question: A Prince George store sells 3000 phone chargers a month. Testing a charger means heating it until it fails, so it cannot be sold after. A tester checks 60 chargers and 3 of them fail. Which statement is best supported?
options: About 150 of the 3000 chargers would likely fail
All 3000 chargers should be heated and checked first
Exactly 5% of the 3000 chargers are broken right now
Exactly 3 of the 3000 chargers sold will fail
questions.explain: 3 out of 60 is 5%, and 5% of 3000 is about 150. A sample gives an estimate, not an exact count, and heating all 3000 would destroy the whole stock.

questions.question: A Kamloops city worker needs the average number of people per household for 12 000 homes, but visiting them all would take months. She visits 200 homes and finds 500 people living in them. Which conclusion is sensible?
options: Exactly 500 people live in the 12 000 homes counted
The mean is about 2.5, so roughly 30 000 people
She must visit all 12 000 homes to say anything
The mean is 2.5, so exactly 30 000 people live there
questions.explain: 500 people in 200 homes gives a mean of 2.5 per home, and 2.5 times 12 000 is roughly 30 000. Sample results estimate the population, so the total is approximate, not exact.

questions.question: A news post says “A survey of 40 shoppers at one Richmond mall shows 90% of British Columbians prefer online shopping.” Why is this headline misleading?
options: Because 36 out of 40 shoppers is not 90 percent
Because 40 shoppers must equal all British Columbians first
Because 40 mall shoppers cannot speak for the province
Because every British Columbian could easily be surveyed instead
questions.explain: 36 out of 40 really is 90%, so the percent is right, but one mall's 40 shoppers are too few and too narrow a group to describe all of BC, which is what makes the claim misleading.

questions.question: A Vancouver library has 4000 members. A librarian wants to know the mean number of books a member borrows in a year. She looks at the records of 100 members and finds a mean of 12 books. Which statement describes this study correctly?
options: The 100 chosen are the population; the 4000 members are the sample.
Every one of the 4000 members borrows exactly 12 books each year.
A mean is only true if all 4000 records are read, so read them all.
The 4000 members are the population; the 100 chosen are the sample.
questions.explain: The population is the whole group you want to know about (all 4000 members), and the sample is the smaller group actually checked (the 100 records). The common trap is turning the sample mean of 12 books into a fact about every single member.

questions.question: A Kelowna teacher needs two numbers: the mean height of the 26 students in her own class, and the mean height of all 2400 Grade 9 students in the district. Which plan is the sensible one?
options: Measure all 26 in her class, but sample from the 2400 students.
Measure every student in both groups, since a census is possible.
Measure her 26 students and report that as the district mean.
Take a sample for both groups; counting everyone is always slow.
questions.explain: When a group is small enough to check quickly, measure everyone; sample only when checking all of them would cost too much time or money. The trap is using one class of 26 as if it were the whole district of 2400.

questions.question: A Delta factory makes 5000 bike locks a day. Testing a lock means cutting it with a power saw, so a tested lock is ruined and cannot be sold. Why can the factory not test every lock it makes?
options: A company should test all of its stock, since a census is always possible.
Cutting open every lock would leave the factory with no locks to sell.
Results from a few locks already prove every lock is exactly the same.
Locks made on the same day are identical, so no testing is needed at all.
questions.explain: When the test destroys the item, checking the whole population leaves nothing behind, so testing a small sample is the only sensible choice. The trap is thinking a few tested locks prove every lock is the same — a sample gives an estimate, not a guarantee.

questions.question: A Nanaimo council wants the mean weight of the garbage each of its 15 000 households throws out. Weighing every household would need 40 extra workers and cost thousands of dollars, so the council weighs the garbage of 150 households. Which statement best explains this choice?
options: The 150 households show exactly what all 15 000 households do.
Sampling works only because 150 divides evenly into 15 000.
A sample of 150 gives a good estimate for far less time and money.
Council should weigh all 15 000, since a census is always possible.
questions.explain: Sampling is the sensible choice when a census would cost too much time or money, and 150 households give a close estimate for the 15 000. The trap is saying the 150 results are exactly true for every household.
